```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

A fitted mixture model is evaluated on four questions: whether the estimation
found a stable solution, how clearly observations and groups are classified,
whether the indicators are independent within profiles as the model assumes,
and whether a different number of profiles or group classes fits better.
These questions follow current guidance for latent profile analysis (Spurk et
al., 2020; Scrucca et al., 2024), and they matter because the profiles of a
person-centred model are interpreted as substantive subgroups (Saqr et al.,
2024). This guide shows the functions that answer each of them for a
two-level model.

## Data

`course_engagement` has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from
106 students. `student` identifies the group, and five activity measures
(`browse`, `lectures`, `forum_read`, `forum_post`, `attendance`) are the
indicators, each standardized within course.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

## The model to evaluate

`multilpa()` fits the model, with `vars` for the indicators, `id` for the
group, `n_profiles` for the number of profiles, `n_group_classes` for the
number of group classes, `n_starts` for the number of random EM starts, and
`seed` for reproducible starts. The model evaluated first uses the default
diagonal covariance structure.

```{r fit}
fit <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                         "attendance"),
                id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
```

## Estimation

`get_results()` with `"model"` reports the convergence of the fit. `converged`
reports convergence of the best start, `boundary` whether a variance reached
its lower bound, and `n_best_replicated` how many starts reached the best log
likelihood. A variance at its lower bound in a profile of about one
observation is a degenerate solution; fitting with `boundary = "exclude"`
keeps the best start without one. A profile with fewer effective members than
its own means and variances raises a `latents_thin_profiles` warning: its
variances are poorly determined, so inspect its covariance diagnostics before
interpreting it.

```{r model}
get_results(fit, "model")
```

`get_results()` with `"starts"` reports every start.

```{r starts}
get_results(fit, "starts")
```

`sensitivity()` refits the model from the seeds given in `seeds` and reports
whether they reach the same solution. `optimum` numbers the
distinct maxima found, and `agreement` is the share of observations assigned
as in the original fit, after matching the arbitrary profile labels.

```{r sensitivity}
sensitivity(fit, seeds = 1:3)
```

All three starts and all three seeds reach the log likelihood of -8440 with
identical assignments, so the solution does not depend on the starting
values.

## Classification

`get_results()` with `"entropy"` reports the relative entropy (Ramaswamy et
al., 1993) for observations and for groups: 1 means every case is assigned
with certainty, 0 means no separation.

```{r entropy}
get_results(fit, "entropy")
```

`get_results()` with `"classification"` reports the classification quality
of every class. `n_modal` is the number of cases assigned to the class,
`average_posterior` the mean posterior probability of those cases, and
`odds_correct_classification` compares that certainty with the class's size
(Nagin, 2005).

```{r classification}
get_results(fit, "classification")
```

Relative entropy is 0.938 for the enrolments and 0.940 for the students, and
the average posterior probabilities of the two profiles are 0.985 and 0.982:
the classification is clear at both levels.

`plot_diagnostics()` draws the uncertainty: `what = "entropy"` the per-case
uncertainty within each profile, and `what = "avepp"` the average posterior of
each assigned class across all classes.

```{r entropy-plot}
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "entropy")
```

```{r avepp-plot}
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "avepp")
```

## Local independence

The default model assumes the indicators are independent within a profile.
`get_results()` with `"residuals"` tests this: `residual` is the correlation
between two indicators that the profiles leave unexplained, and
`by = "overall"` pools the profiles. The p-values are approximate and are
adjusted for multiple testing (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

```{r residuals}
get_results(fit, "residuals", by = "overall")
```

The four largest residuals all involve `attendance` (0.17 to 0.22, adjusted
p-values below 0.001), so the assumption does not hold for these data;
`attendance` is generated from the four click measures
(`?course_engagement`). `covariance_model = "full"` relaxes the assumption by
estimating the covariances between indicators within each profile, and
`get_results()` with `"information_criteria"` compares the two models; lower
values are better.

```{r full-covariance}
full <- multilpa(course_engagement,
                 vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                          "attendance"),
                 id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2,
                 covariance_model = "full", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(fit, "information_criteria")
get_results(full, "information_criteria")
get_results(full, "residuals", by = "overall")
```

The full model lowers the BIC with students as units from 16,987 to 16,827.
Its residuals are zero, because it estimates every within-profile covariance;
the residual check is informative only for a model that restricts them. The
full model is the one to evaluate further.

## Number of profiles and group classes

`enumerate_classes()` compares numbers of profiles and group classes, with
`n_profiles` and `n_group_classes` for the counts to cross. It crosses the counts with four covariance structures, equal or
varying variances with and without covariances, fits every combination, and
does not choose a model.

```{r enumerate}
candidates <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement,
                                vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read",
                                         "forum_post", "attendance"),
                                id = "student", n_profiles = 2:4,
                                n_group_classes = 1:3, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
subset(as.data.frame(candidates), model == "VVV")
```

`get_results()` with `"best"` gives the candidate that minimizes each
criterion. Criteria that depend on a sample size are reported with the
number of groups and with the number of observations.

```{r best}
get_results(candidates, "best")
```

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) with students as units is lowest for two profiles,
three group classes and the `VVV` structure, and most criteria select two
profiles with a structure that estimates covariances. The
[Class enumeration](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/enumeration.html)
article examines the choice between two and three group classes on these
data.

`plot_enumeration()` draws one criterion across the grid, named in `what`;
`what = "all"` draws every criterion.

```{r enumeration-plot}
plot_enumeration(candidates, what = "bic_groups")
```

`get_candidate()` takes one candidate out of the grid as a fitted model,
given by its `n_profiles`, `n_group_classes` and `model`.

```{r candidate}
get_candidate(candidates, n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 3, model = "VVV")
```

## Parameter uncertainty

`parameter_inference()` returns standard errors and 95% Wald intervals; with
`vcov_type = "robust"`, the standard errors are clustered on groups. The first
ten rows of each, for the full model:

```{r inference}
head(parameter_inference(full), 10)
head(parameter_inference(full, vcov_type = "robust"), 10)
```

## Reference

The calls below list other evaluation functions and views. Each comment states
what the call returns.

```{r reference, eval = FALSE}
get_results(fit, "information_criteria", format = "long")  # one row per criterion
get_results(fit, "average_posteriors")          # mean posterior by assigned class
get_results(fit, "classification_errors")       # P(assigned class | true class)
get_results(fit, "residuals")                   # residuals within each profile
get_results(candidates, "candidates")           # the full enumeration grid
summary(candidates)                             # every grid table, truncated
bootstrap_lrt(full, get_candidate(candidates, n_profiles = 2,
                                 n_group_classes = 3, model = "VVV"),
              iter = 199, seed = 42)            # bootstrap test of one more class (slow)
enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = c("browse", "lectures"),
                  id = "student", n_profiles = 2:3,
                  model = c("VVI", "VVV"))      # crossing covariance models (slow)
confint(fit)                                    # confidence intervals
vcov(fit, vcov_type = "robust")                 # robust covariance matrix
plot_diagnostics(fit, what = "posteriors")                  # posterior of each assigned profile
plot_profiles(fit, what = "bars")                        # profile means with 95% intervals
diagnostics(fit)                                # all classification diagnostics
```

## Limits

- Information criteria compare the candidates fitted, not all possible models.
- Classification measures describe the fitted model; a misspecified model can
  still classify sharply.
- Wald intervals assume a converged fit with no variance at its bound, and are
  conditional on the chosen numbers of profiles and classes.
- Unmodelled dependence between indicators can make extra classes look better.
